1
Network-Native DNN Architecture Synthesis for
Distributed Inference
Fan Yang, Xiaolong Wu, Qi Cao, Fen Hou, Yulin Shao
Abstract—Distributed deep neural network (DNN) inference
typically follows a model-first paradigm, in which a predefined
DNN is partitioned and deployed over a physical network.
On irregular communication-computation topologies, however,
this approach can create transmission bottlenecks and leave
distributed resources underutilized. This paper reverses this
perspective and asks: given a physical network, what kind of DNN
can it naturally support? To answer this question, we propose
a network-native DNN architecture synthesis paradigm in which
the physical network topology directly defines inter-node neural
dependencies. Neural computation is allocated across nodes
under communication, computation, storage, synchronization,
and latency constraints. We establish structural properties of
the synthesis problem and develop linear programming (LP)-
based Architecture Synthesis (LPAS), an efficient topology-
guided algorithm that produces a feasible architecture with a
computable bound on suboptimality. Experiments on physical
networks of different sizes show that LPAS achieves relative gaps
below 0.6% to the LP-derived upper bound, with substantially
lower runtime than direct mixed-integer LP optimization on
larger networks. Under matched network deadlines, the network-
native architectures activate more compute nodes and utilize a
larger proportion of available model-storage capacity than the
model-first baseline. After training, the network-native models
achieve higher classification accuracy across all evaluated dataset-
precision settings, with the average gain of up to 10.69%.
This network-native design paradigm thus turns the physical
network from a deployment constraint into an architecture design
primitive.
Index Terms—Distributed inference, neural architecture syn-
thesis, in-network AI, communication-computation networks.
I. INTRODUCTION
The growing availability of computing resources across
end devices, edge servers, access points, and programmable
network devices [1], [2] creates new opportunities for dis-
tributed deep neural network (DNN) inference [3]. By execut-
ing a DNN collaboratively across multiple networked nodes,
distributed inference can pool fragmented computation and
storage resources, reduce the burden on individual devices,
and avoid dependence on a single execution point [4].
Against this backdrop, a natural question has dominated
much of the existing literature: Given a DNN, how should
it be partitioned and deployed onto a physical network? This
question has motivated a broad range of research on DNN
F. Yang and F. Hou are with the State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things
for Smart City, University of Macau, Macao, China.
X. Wu and Y. Shao are with the Department of Electrical and Computer
Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China.
Qi Cao is with Xidian-Guangzhou Research Institute, Xidian University,
Guangzhou, China.
partitioning, collaborative inference, split computing, and in-
network AI. The prevailing deployment scenarios include two-
tier device-cloud systems [5], [6], multi-node edge execution
and pipeline parallelism [7], [8], and hierarchical or graph-
structured execution [9]–[11]. These approaches generally
specify the neural architecture first and then optimize its
partitioning, placement, and execution over the network. We
refer to this design pattern as the model-first deployment
paradigm.
On irregular communication-computation topologies, a
fixed neural dependency graph can remain restrictive even
after deployment is optimized. Placement and routing deci-
sions determine where prescribed computations execute and
how their features are transmitted, but generally preserve the
DNN’s dependencies. These dependencies can concentrate
execution on a limited set of nodes and links while leaving
resources on other branches underutilized. We refer to this
incompatibility between the neural computational graph and
the physical network as topological mismatch.
In such a setting, the physical network is not merely a
passive container for a pre-designed model. Its topology, com-
puting capabilities, link characteristics, and synchronization
structure actively constrain and shape the forms of neural
computation that can be executed efficiently. This observation
motivates us to ask the inverse question:
Given a physical network, what kind of DNN can it
naturally support?
We address this question by proposing network-native DNN
architecture synthesis. Rather than first designing a DNN and
then searching for a deployment strategy, this approach starts
from the physical communication-computation network and
constructs a neural architecture aligned with it. We model
the physical network as a directed acyclic graph (DAG),
whose topology defines the inter-node neural dependencies of
the synthesized architecture. Node computation speeds, link
delays, and storage capacities further determine the placement
and amount of neural computation. The resulting model is
therefore not a conventional DNN partitioned across multiple
devices, but a network-native architecture synthesized for
the underlying communication-computation substrate. Fig. 1
illustrates the distinction between the two paradigms.
We synthesize architectures for a single inference request
under a prescribed network-execution deadline and subse-
quently train them end-to-end for the target task. Our main
contributions are summarized as follows.
• We propose a network-native DNN architecture synthesis
paradigm that fundamentally departs from conventional

Figure 1.
Comparison between model-first deployment and network-native DNN architecture synthesis. (a) A predefined DNN is mapped onto a selected
route, illustrating topological mismatch through unused physical nodes and branches. (b) The synthesized architecture follows the physical topology in its
inter-node neural dependencies, while network resources constrain the allocation of neural computation.
model-first distributed inference. Instead of partitioning and
deploying a predefined DNN over a physical network, we
construct a DNN whose inter-node neural dependencies
are directly determined by the physical communication-
computation topology. By treating the network as a directed
acyclic graph (DAG), we formulate a resource-constrained
architecture synthesis problem that maximizes the number
of trainable neural modules, as a proxy for model capacity,
while accounting for computation, communication, storage,
synchronization, and end-to-end latency constraints.
• We establish structural properties of the architecture syn-
thesis problem that enable efficient optimization with the-
oretical guarantees. In particular, we characterize inference
latency through longest paths on the physical DAG and
derive an liner programming (LP)-based upper bound on
the optimal number of neural modules. Building on these
results, we develop LP-based architecture synthesis (LPAS),
a polynomial-time algorithm that combines feasibility-
preserving rounding with latency-aware greedy module
allocation. LPAS guarantees a feasible architecture and
provides a computable bound on its objective suboptimality,
without requiring exact mixed-integer optimization.
• We demonstrate the computational efficiency and practical
benefits of network-native architecture synthesis through
extensive evaluations across different physical network
topologies and DNN configurations. LPAS achieves mean
relative gaps below 0.6% to the LP-derived upper bound
while substantially reducing runtime compared with direct
mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) optimization on
larger networks. Under matched network-execution dead-
lines, the synthesized architectures exploit more distributed
computing and storage resources than an optimized model-
first deployment baseline. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and
CIFAR-100 further show higher classification accuracy
across all evaluated dataset-precision settings, with gains
of up to 10.69%.
II. RELATED WORK
Distributed DNN inference has been extensively studied
under the model-first paradigm [1], [3]. Early device-cloud
systems, such as Neurosurgeon [5] and JointDNN [6], deter-
mine how a predefined DNN should be partitioned between
two endpoints based on execution profiles, latency, and energy
considerations.
As distributed inference extends to multiple devices, de-
ployment decisions must also account for computation place-
ment and data-transfer paths [12], [13]. This has led to joint
optimization of DNN partition deployment and computing-
resource allocation in MEC networks [7], as well as layered-
graph formulations that capture computation-node and data-
transfer-path selection [14]. For heterogeneous edge devices,
pipeline-based approaches assign predefined stages to devices
[8] or jointly optimize device-to-stage assignment and inter-
and intra-layer partitioning to improve inference throughput
[15].
More complex distributed inference settings involve hier-
archical collaboration and DNNs with nonsequential com-
putational dependencies [16]. Hierarchical and cooperative
approaches distribute jointly trained model components across
device-edge-cloud systems [9] or adaptively partition DNN
workloads across heterogeneous edge devices [17]. When the
DNN itself contains parallel branches and merges, deployment
must also preserve dependencies among computations that
may execute on different devices. For these DAG-structured
DNNs, existing work addresses dependency-aware execution
[10], equivalent chain representations for streaming partition-
ing and offloading [18], and joint operator-grained partitioning,


--- Page 3 ---
3
offloading, and resource allocation in multi-user MEC systems
[19].
Beyond deployment optimization, some studies modify
DNN architectures to improve distributed execution. DFSNet
transforms conventional DNNs into dividing-fuse architectures
through channel-wise partitioning and sparse fusion, with fu-
sion positions selected through search [20]. Other approaches
restructure, partition, and prune pretrained DNNs to reduce
dependencies among sub-models [21], or incorporate network-
dependent communication costs into DNN pruning [22].
Neural architecture search (NAS) provides another approach
to DNN architecture design by exploring candidate structures
within a predefined search space. Hardware-aware methods,
such as MnasNet [23] and ProxylessNAS [24], incorporate
device-dependent performance into the selection of operators,
blocks, widths, and depths. When DNN inference extends
across multiple devices, architecture design must also consider
how neural computation is distributed and how intermediate
features are transmitted. For example, LENS incorporates
communication-dependent latency and energy into architec-
ture search for edge-cloud systems [25], while SplitNets
jointly considers architecture design, model splitting, and
communication reduction in sensor-aggregator systems [26].
The coupling between architecture search and deployment is
further explored in different ways. JMSNAS searches candi-
date operations under task-loss and network-latency objectives
with a predefined computational graph and device-wise layer
partitions [27], whereas GCoDE jointly searches graph neural
network architectures and operation mappings across device-
edge systems [28].
Existing studies range from deploying predefined DNNs
to adapting or searching neural architectures under system
constraints. In contrast, network-native DNN architecture syn-
thesis uses the physical communication-computation DAG
to directly define the inter-node neural dependencies of the
synthesized architecture: physical branches and merges define
neural branches and fusion points. This network-defined struc-
ture leads to a constrained module-allocation problem whose
DAG properties support explicit latency analysis and efficient
architecture synthesis with feasibility and gap guarantees.
III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
We consider the synthesis of a DNN architecture and its exe-
cution over a prescribed physical communication-computation
network. The physical network is modeled as a DAG G =
(V, E), where V is the set of physical nodes and E is the set
of directed communication links.
A source node S ∈V receives the input sample, and a sink
node T ∈V produces the final output. For a specific learning
task, fixed input and output interfaces map the raw input to
the common feature space and map the terminal feature or
features to the task output, respectively. These interfaces are
not architecture-synthesis variables. We therefore define the
modeled execution interval to begin when the common input
feature becomes available at S and to end when all features
required by the output interface have arrived at T.
Accordingly, S and T serve as the boundary nodes of the
distributed architecture, while neural computation modules are
assigned only to the intermediate nodes. Let I = V \ {S, T}
denote the set of intermediate compute nodes, and let N = |I|.
We assume that every physical node lies on at least one
directed path from S to T; any node that violates this condition
can be removed without affecting the modeled inference
execution.
For every v ∈V, let dv = |{u : (u, v) ∈E}| denote its
in-degree. Each intermediate node v ∈I is characterized by a
computation-delay coefficient Av > 0 and an available model-
storage capacity Mv ≥0. The coefficient Av is measured in
seconds per unit computation; hence, a smaller Av corresponds
to a faster compute node. Each directed link (u, v) ∈E is
characterized by a communication-delay coefficient Buv > 0,
measured in seconds per unit transmitted data. Equivalently,
Buv is the reciprocal of the effective transmission rate of the
link. Consequently, transmitting a feature of data size D over
link (u, v) incurs a delay of BuvD. Different physical links
are assumed to be independently provisioned, so simultaneous
transmissions on distinct links do not contend for communi-
cation resources.
A. Modular Architecture Design
For a given task, the basic neural module, feature repre-
sentation, and fusion operator are selected before synthesis.
The physical DAG determines the inter-node computational
dependencies, while node-wise module allocation determines
the amount of neural computation. We adopt the following
modular design assumptions.
1) All features transmitted over the edges of G have the same
data size D.
2) An intermediate node begins its local processing only
after all incoming features have arrived.
3) The trainable architecture on a node is constructed from
repeated instances of a dimension-preserving neural mod-
ule (see Definition 1).
4) Transmissions over distinct outgoing links proceed in
parallel (in a multicast fashion).
Definition 1 (Module). A module is a neural computation unit
that maps an input feature of size D to an output feature of the
same size D. It can be instantiated using a standard neural
building block, such as a residual block [29], a self-attention
block [30], or a depthwise-separable convolution block [31].
For a fixed module primitive and feature shape, let F > 0
denote the computation required by one module. The value
of F can be derived analytically from the selected neural
operators or obtained through offline profiling. Once the
module primitive and feature shape have been selected, F is
fixed throughout the architecture synthesis problem.
Each intermediate physical node can host a sequential stack
of repeated modules. For v ∈I, let Lv ∈Z≥0 denote the
number of modules assigned to node v. The complete module
allocation is represented by L = (Lv)v∈I. For notational
convenience, we extend the allocation to the boundary nodes
using LS = LT = 0.
The local processing performed at an intermediate node con-
sists of an optional fusion operation followed by its assigned

Figure 2. Execution at an intermediate node. (a) Node-level synchronization, fusion, module execution, and output replication. (b) Timing of incoming feature
arrivals, node computation, and independent outgoing transmissions.
module stack. If dv = 1, the single incoming feature is passed
directly to the local modules. If dv > 1, the incoming features
are first fused into one feature of size D. The fusion operator is
selected before synthesis rather than optimized during module
allocation.
Let Gv ≥0 denote the fixed computation cost of the pre-
scribed fusion operation at node v, with Gv = 0 when dv = 1.
For a merging node, Gv may depend on the feature shape, the
in-degree dv, and the selected fusion implementation, but is
independent of the module allocation Lv.
The processing delay at an intermediate node v ∈I is
therefore ∆v(Lv) = Av(FLv +Gv). For the boundary nodes,
we use the convention ∆S(LS) = ∆T (LT ) = 0.
After completing its local processing, an intermediate node
replicates its output feature and transmits one copy over each
outgoing link. The replication itself introduces no additional
neural computation, while the transmission delay is accounted
for separately on each link.
The physical DAG remains fixed throughout synthesis. In
particular, setting Lv = 0 removes only the repeated module
stack at node v; it does not deactivate the node or its incident
links. Such a node performs the prescribed fusion operation
when dv > 1, or acts as an identity relay when dv = 1, before
forwarding its output to its child nodes.
B. Resource and Latency Constraints
1) Node Storage Constraint: In practical distributed infer-
ence systems, each physical node has limited storage for neural
model parameters. Therefore, a node cannot host an arbitrarily
large number of modules even if its computation speed is high.
Let Pmod > 0 denote the parameter storage required by
one instance of the selected neural module. As with the per-
module computation F, Pmod can be determined analytically
or through offline profiling and remains fixed during synthesis.
Let Pfus,v ≥0 denote the fixed parameter-storage cost of
the prescribed fusion operation at node v, with Pfus,v = 0
when dv = 1.
The parameter-storage constraint at any intermediate node
v ∈I is LvPmod + Pfus,v ≤Mv.
A feasible instance requires Mv ≥Pfus,v for every v ∈
I. Since Lv is integer, the storage constraint is equivalently
represented by the module-capacity bound
0 ≤Lv ≤Uv ≜
Mv −Pfus,v
Pmod

,
∀v ∈I.
(1)
For notational completeness, we set US = UT = 0. The same
capacity bound is retained in the continuous relaxation. The
storage model accounts only for the parameters of the de-
ployed inference model; activation buffers, temporary operator
workspace, communication buffers, and runtime memory are
assumed to be provisioned separately.
2) Edge-Level Latency Constraint: The primary system-
level requirement is an end-to-end latency deadline TD. For
each intermediate node v ∈I, let tv denote the time at which
its local processing begins. Consistent with the boundary
convention introduced above, tS is the time at which the
common source feature becomes available, while tT is the
time at which all features required by the output interface
have arrived at the sink.
For every directed edge (u, v) ∈E, the feature transmitted
by node u cannot become available at node v before node u
has completed its local computation and transmitted its output
feature. Therefore, the following edge-level timing constraint
must hold:
tv ≥tu + ∆u(Lu) + BuvD,
∀(u, v) ∈E.
(2)
The source node starts at tS = 0. The sink node must be
reached before the deadline: tT ≤TD.
The edge-level formulation automatically captures synchro-


--- Page 5 ---
5
nization at merging nodes. If a node v has multiple incoming
edges, then (2) must hold for every parent u of v. As a result,
tv must be no smaller than the latest arrival time among all
incoming features. Therefore, no additional synchronization
constraint is required for a single inference request. The com-
plete execution flow of an intermediate node is summarized
in Fig. 2.
C. The Architecture Synthesis Problem
We next specify the objective of architecture synthesis.
Prior studies on deep residual networks and CNN scaling
have shown that increasing model depth and size can improve
task performance under suitable architectural and training
conditions [29], [32]. Research on neural scaling laws further
highlights the relationship between model scale and learning
performance [33]. These findings motivate a capacity-oriented
design that exploits the available network resources to con-
struct larger trainable models.
In this modular design, each module contributes the same
computation F and parameter storage Pmod, while fusion costs
are fixed independently of the module allocation. Thus, the
total number of modules directly determines the aggregate
computation and parameter count of the trainable module
stacks. We therefore use the network-wide module budget
Z(L) = P
v∈I Lv as a tractable proxy for the representational
capacity of the synthesized architecture and maximize it under
the physical-network constraints. The task performance of the
resulting architectures is subsequently evaluated after training.
The architecture synthesis problem is therefore to determine
how many modules should be instantiated at each intermediate
node while satisfying the node-capacity and end-to-end latency
requirements. Formally, we seek a module allocation L and a
feasible set of node start times {tv}v∈V according to
max
L, {tv}v∈V
Z(L)
s.t.
tv ≥tu + ∆u(Lu) + BuvD,
∀(u, v) ∈E,
tS = 0,
tT ≤TD,
0 ≤Lv ≤Uv,
Lv ∈Z≥0,
∀v ∈I.
(3)
The physical DAG fixes the inter-node connectivity, whereas
L determines the trainable capacity placed at each intermediate
node. The constraints capture computation, communication,
synchronization, and storage dependencies. Because ∆v(Lv)
is affine in Lv and the allocation variables are integer-valued,
the design formulation in (3) admits a MILP representation.
This representation provides a computational means of synthe-
sizing DNN architectures; the underlying architectural ques-
tion is how the trainable neural capacity should be distributed
over a given physical communication-computation network.
IV. STRUCTURAL PROPERTIES OF THE SYNTHESIS
PROBLEM
The design of LPAS relies on two key ingredients: a bound
on the optimal module budget and efficient methods for con-
structing and evaluating feasible allocations. We first establish
an LP-derived upper bound and characterize allocation fea-
sibility through longest-path recursions on the physical DAG.
These results then enable a feasible floor-rounded initialization
and an exact test for one-module extensions.
A. Continuous Relaxation and LP Upper Bound
Removing the integrality requirement from (3) while retain-
ing all other constraints gives the continuous relaxation

and define Z⋆

Proof. Condition (13) is necessary and sufficient for the node-

v by AvF, while all other edge weights remain unchanged.
The maximum latency of a source-to-sink path passing
through v is θL
S (v)+θL
T (v). Since G is acyclic, the maximizing
source-to-v path and v-to-sink path cannot share any node
other than v. They can therefore be concatenated into a valid
source-to-sink path. Therefore,
T(L(v)) = max

T(L), θL
S (v) + θL
T (v) + AvF
	
.
(15)
Because L is feasible, T(L) ≤TD. Therefore, by (15), the
extended allocation satisfies the latency deadline if and only
if (14) holds.
Proposition 3 tests each one-module extension without enu-
merating source-to-sink paths. For a fixed feasible allocation,
one forward and one reverse topological traversal suffice to
identify all feasible one-module extensions in O(|V| + |E|)
time.
V. EFFICIENT LP-BASED ARCHITECTURE SYNTHESIS
Building on the structural properties established in Sec-
tion IV, we develop an efficient synthesis method called LP-
based Architecture Synthesis (LPAS). The method first solves
the continuous relaxation and rounds its solution down to
obtain a feasible integer module allocation. Starting from this
allocation, LPAS repeatedly adds one module at a time using
the exact feasibility test in Proposition 3. Each iteration selects
the feasible extension with the smallest resulting end-to-end
latency.
A. Initialization
LPAS begins by solving the continuous relaxation in (4).
If the relaxation is infeasible, the integer problem is also
infeasible, and the method terminates.
Otherwise, let LLP denote an optimal relaxed allocation,
and recall the integer upper bound ZUB = ⌊Z⋆
LP⌋. The initial
integer allocation is obtained by componentwise floor round-
ing as L0 = ⌊LLP⌋, with Z0 = Z(L0). By Proposition 2, L0
is feasible for the integer problem.
We define Kmax ≜ZUB−Z0. By (10), 0 ≤Kmax ≤N −1.
If the LP has multiple optimal solutions, any optimal alloca-
tion may be used. The resulting initialization and architecture
may vary, but the guarantees below hold for every such
choice. Given an initialization, a fixed node ordering makes
the padding deterministic.
B. Greedy Padding
For a current feasible integer allocation L, let C(L) ⊆I
contain the nodes satisfying both the capacity test in (13) and
the latency test in (14). Proposition 3 makes this exactly the
set of feasible one-module extensions.
The resulting end-to-end latency T(L(v)) of each candidate
extension can be evaluated exactly using (15).

7

3: Solve the LP relaxation in (4)
4: if the LP relaxation is infeasible then

7: ˆL ←⌊LLP⌋

Starting from the allocation L0, LPAS selects v⋆
∈
arg minv∈C(L) T(L(v)), resolves ties by the fixed node order-
ing, and updates L ←L + ev⋆. The forward and reverse
longest-path values are recomputed at the start of each subse-
quent padding iteration. The procedure stops when C(L) = ∅
or the module budget reaches ZUB, returning ˆL.
Remark (Beam Search). The padding stage can be extended
to a beam-search variant by retaining up to W > 1 feasible
candidate allocations at each iteration instead of a single
one. Each retained allocation generates its feasible one-
module extensions, from which up to W candidates with the
smallest resulting end-to-end latencies are selected for the
next iteration. When W = 1, this procedure reduces to the
greedy padding strategy described above. We adopt W = 1
in this work to avoid maintaining and evaluating multiple
candidate allocations, thereby keeping the algorithm simple
and computationally efficient.
C. Algorithm, Guarantees, and Complexity
For the returned allocation, define the LP-induced upper-
bound gap as GUB ≜ZUB −Z(ˆL). Algorithm 1 summarizes
the complete procedure.
Proposition 4 (LPAS Guarantees). Suppose that the LP re-
laxation is feasible and N ≥1. The allocation ˆL returned by
LPAS is feasible for (3) and satisfies
0 ≤Z⋆
MILP −Z(ˆL) ≤GUB ≤Kmax ≤N −1.
(16)
Proof. The initial allocation L0 is feasible by Proposition 2.
Every subsequent allocation is obtained using a feasible one-
module extension identified by Proposition 3, so ˆL is feasible.
Hence, Z(ˆL) ≤Z⋆
MILP.
Since LPAS only inserts modules into L0, we have Z0 ≤
Z(ˆL) ≤ZUB. Together with Z⋆
MILP ≤ZUB, this gives
0 ≤Z⋆
MILP −Z(ˆL) ≤GUB ≤ZUB −Z0 = Kmax.
(17)
Finally, combining (17) with the bound Kmax ≤N −1 from
(10) establishes the claimed result.
Thus, GUB provides a computable upper bound on the
objective loss, and GUB = 0 certifies global optimality.
Computational complexity. Let n = |V|, m = |E|, and N =
|I| = n−2. Let CLP denote the computational cost of solving
the LP relaxation. The componentwise floor rounding of LLP
requires O(N) time.
At each padding iteration, one forward and one reverse
topological traversal compute θL
S and θL
T in O(n + m) time.
Once these values are available, the feasibility and resulting
latency of each of the at most N one-module extensions can
be evaluated in constant time. Selecting the feasible extension
with the minimum resulting latency requires an additional
O(N) scan. Since N ≤n, the overall cost of one padding
iteration is O(n + m).
The padding stage performs at most Kmax ≤N −1
successful module additions and may require one additional
iteration to detect that no feasible extension remains. Hence,
its total computational cost is O((Kmax + 1)(n + m)) =
O(N(n + m)) . Including the LP relaxation and floor round-
ing, the overall complexity of LPAS is CLPAS = CLP +
O(N(n + m)) .
The LP relaxation has polynomial size in the problem in-
stance, and linear programming is solvable in polynomial time.
Therefore, LPAS is a polynomial-time synthesis algorithm
that returns a feasible architecture with a computable bound
on objective suboptimality, without requiring an exact MILP
solution.
VI. MODEL-FIRST BASELINE: LAYERED-GRAPH
DEPLOYMENT
To compare network-native architecture synthesis with
model-first deployment, we construct a baseline optimized
over the same physical network. We consider the deployment
of a complete predefined DNN over G
= (V, E), while
preserving its operations and data dependencies. Following
the layered-graph formulation in [14], we adapt the state-
space construction to the ordered execution-unit profiles and
physical-DAG setting considered here, and refer to the result-
ing baseline as layered-graph deployment (LGD).
A. Complete Reference-DNN Profile
To optimize the deployment of a predefined DNN, we
first represent its computation and communication costs at
valid partition boundaries. The complete reference DNN is
profiled offline as an ordered sequence of deployable execution
units Q = (q1, q2, . . . , qJ), whose boundaries preserve the
operations and data dependencies of the original model. An
execution unit may be an individual layer or a composite block
containing a residual or multi-branch subgraph.
Each unit qk is characterized by its computation workload
Fk and parameter storage Pk. Let Dk denote the aggregate
size of the boundary state after units q1, . . . , qk have been
completed, including any intermediate features required by
subsequent units, where D0 and DJ denote the raw-input and

final-output sizes, respectively. The profile spans the complete
reference DNN, from its first model operation through the
final classifier, and no execution unit is removed before
deployment. Parameter-free operations are retained through
their computation and boundary-state contributions.
LGD deploys Q over one directed source-to-sink path in
G. Each intermediate node executes a consecutive segment of
Q or forwards the current boundary state without local DNN
computation. The source and sink do not execute reference-
DNN units; all units in Q are assigned to intermediate compute
nodes.
B. Layered-Graph Deployment
LGD constructs a layered DAG in which state (v, k) indi-
cates that the first k execution units have been completed and
that the corresponding boundary state is available at physical
node v. The initial and terminal states are (S, 0) and (T, J),
respectively.
For each physical link (u, v) ∈E with v ∈I, a tran-
sition (u, i) →(v, j), 0 ≤i ≤j ≤J, is introduced
when the segment qi+1, . . . , qj satisfies the storage constraint
Pj
k=i+1 Pk ≤Mv. The transition transmits the boundary state
after qi to node v and executes the corresponding segment
at v, with weight cij
uv
= BuvDi + Av
Pj
k=i+1 Fk. The
case i = j represents pure forwarding. For a physical link
(u, T) ∈E, the terminal transition (u, J) →(T, J) has weight
cJJ
uT = BuT DJ.
Fig. 3 illustrates the layered-state construction and how a
source-to-sink path jointly specifies the physical route and the
consecutive DNN segments executed along that route.
Because the physical network is a DAG, the layered graph
is also acyclic. Let PLGD denote the set of directed paths from
(S, 0) to (T, J). The minimum LGD deployment latency is

O(|E|J2) transitions. Using prefix sums of {Fk} and {Pk},

For each reference DNN with a feasible LGD deployment,
we use its optimal LGD latency to define the network-
execution deadline for the resulting network-native architec-
ture as
TD = T ⋆
LGD.
(19)
Thus, LGD and LPAS operate over the same physical network
under a matched network deadline: the model-first baseline
optimizes the deployment of the complete predefined DNN
within the LGD design space, whereas LPAS synthesizes a
network-native architecture subject to the resulting deadline.
VII. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
This section evaluates network-native DNN architecture
synthesis from both algorithmic and paradigm-level perspec-
tives. We first examine the solution quality, computational cost,
and stability of LPAS over physical DAGs of different scales.
We then compare the network-native architectures with the
model-first LGD baseline under matched network deadlines
and examine how the two paradigms utilize the available dis-
tributed resources. Finally, we compare classification accuracy
on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 across topologies, reference
DNNs, and nominal precision settings.
A. Experimental Setup
We consider the three physical DAGs shown in Fig. 4:
a butterfly-like DAG with six compute nodes, a Nobel-US-
derived DAG with 14 compute nodes, and a Nobel-EU-
derived DAG with 28 compute nodes. The latter two are DAG
variants derived from the Nobel-US and Nobel-EU benchmark
instances in SNDlib, with the directed edges used in our
evaluation shown explicitly in Fig. 4. For brevity, we refer
to the butterfly-like, Nobel-US-derived, and Nobel-EU-derived
DAGs as Butterfly, Nobel-US, and Nobel-EU, respectively,
throughout the remainder of this paper.

Unless otherwise stated, heterogeneous resources are inde-
pendently sampled from the same ranges for all three topolo-
gies. Node computation throughput is uniformly sampled from
15-60 GFLOP/s, node model-storage capacity from 3-22 MiB,
and physical-link rate from 50-300 Mbps. A fixed random seed
is used only for reproducibility. The common physical-network
and architecture synthesis settings are summarized in Table I.
Each

is
instantiated
as
a
dimension-
preserving MobileLatentBlock (MLB). At an intermediate
compute node with multiple incoming branches, an Atten-
tionFusionBlock (AFB) combines the synchronized parent
features. Its computation and storage requirements depend on
the number of incoming branches and are included in the
corresponding node constraints. At the sink, the fixed output
interface aggregates the incoming features before classifica-
tion. This interface lies outside the modeled network-execution
interval. The integer module capacity of each intermediate
compute node is determined after accounting for its fusion
storage.
For the model-first baseline, we use complete profiles of
ResNet18 [29], DenseNet121 [34], and ResNet50 [29], with
FP16 representations for parameter storage and intermediate
feature transmission. Their profiles contain 46, 132, and 108
deployable execution units, respectively. As described in Sec-
tion VI, LGD deploys the complete reference DNN and returns
its minimum deployment latency T ⋆
LGD.
At the task level, we evaluate network-native architectures
synthesized under deadlines induced by ResNet18, ResNet50,
and DenseNet121, and compare them with the corresponding
model-first baselines on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. For each
topology and reference DNN, the network-native models retain
the same backbone architecture across the two datasets but
use dataset-specific classification heads. All models are ran-
domly initialized and trained from scratch separately on each
dataset, with both the backbone and classification head jointly
optimized. Each network-native model configuration and each
reference DNN configuration is trained three times, and the
highest test accuracy across the three runs is reported.

quantization-aware training (QAT). All models are opti-

warmup followed by linear decay. The peak learning rates for
ResNet18, ResNet50 and DenseNet121 are set to 0.025, 0.03
and 0.05, respectively.
The deadline in (19) is matched within the synthesis model
using the stated resource profiles. The accuracy experiments
do not independently verify end-to-end latency or deadline
feasibility at each nominal precision.
LP relaxation and MILP are solved using MATLAB solvers.
The MILP solutions serve as references in the quality evalu-
ation of the three topologies, while the MILP solver is also
used for runtime comparison in the scalability experiment.

We first isolate the synthesis algorithm from task-level
training and examine whether the LP-floor-greedy procedure
consistently produces high-quality integer solutions with low
computational overhead.

node-wise module-capacity vector U, let Tmin = T(0) and
Tmax = T(U). To cover latency regimes from tight to loose
while excluding the two endpoint cases, we set TD(λ) =

As shown in Table IV, greedy padding reduces the mean
upper-bound gap by approximately half across all three DAGs.
LPAS also maintains low runtime, ranging from 4.52 to 5.08
ms, with a modest increase as the topology grows. These
results demonstrate that LPAS produces high-quality feasible
allocations with little computational overhead on the physical
networks considered in the task-level evaluation.
We further evaluate LPAS on larger randomly generated
physical networks to examine its solution quality and com-
putational scalability. Specifically, we generate single-source
single-sink DAGs with 30 to 70 compute nodes in increments
of 10. For each network size, we consider 50 independent
topology and resource realizations using the same resource
ranges as in Table I. The random DAGs are generated by
distributing compute nodes across ordered layers and establish-
ing forward connections to ensure source-to-sink reachability.
Additional forward edges are randomly added until the total
number of links is approximately 2.5 times the number of com-
pute nodes. For solution quality, we select N ∈{30, 50, 70}
and vary λ from 0.1 to 0.9 in increments of 0.1, reusing the
same realizations across deadlines. We measure the relative
upper-bound gap of LPAS as 100(ZUB −ZLPAS)/ZUB. Since
ZUB is an upper bound on the integer optimum, this metric
also upper-bounds the relative optimality gap. For runtime, we
fix λ = 0.5 and compare LPAS with direct MILP optimization
across all five network sizes. For the scalability experiment,
the MILP solver uses a 10-second time limit and an absolute
optimality-gap tolerance of 0.99 modules.

small relative upper-bound gap across different network sizes

behavior across all three DAGs indicates that LPAS is not
excessively sensitive to moderate perturbations in the compu-
tation and communication parameters.
C. Network-Native Synthesis Versus Model-First Deployment
We next compare network-native architecture synthesis with
model-first deployment under matched network deadlines.
For the paradigm-level comparison, we use one fixed
physical-resource configuration within the ranges in Table I for
each topology and apply it consistently to all three reference
DNNs. No model-specific resource retuning is performed. For
each reference DNN r, LGD first determines its minimum
deployment latency T ⋆
LGD,r, after which LPAS synthesizes a
network-native architecture over the same physical network
with TD,r = T ⋆
LGD,r. Thus, each comparison uses identical
physical-network resources and a matched network deadline,
while differing in whether the DNN architecture is fixed before
deployment or synthesized according to the physical network.

characterize how the two paradigms exploit the distributed
resources. For X ∈{LGD, NNA}, where NNA denotes
the network-native architecture, let I(X)

Figure 7.
Resource utilization of LGD and network-native architectures
under matched deadlines. Top: active compute-node ratio. Bottom: aggregate
model-storage utilization. The three groups from left to right correspond to
Butterfly, Nobel-US, and Nobel-EU. R18, DN121, and R50 denote ResNet18,
DenseNet121, and ResNet50, respectively.
compute-node ratio measures how broadly DNN execution
units or synthesized modules are distributed over the physical
network, whereas the aggregate model-storage utilization mea-
sures the fraction of the total compute-node storage occupied
by the deployed inference model.
For LGD, P (LGD)
dep
includes the complete reference-DNN
parameters deployed on intermediate compute nodes. For the
network-native architecture, P (NNA)
dep
includes all MLBs and
AFBs synthesized on intermediate nodes. The lightweight
input and output interfaces at S and T lie outside the modeled
network-execution interval and are therefore excluded from the
intermediate-node storage accounting.
Figure 7 reveals a consistent structural difference between
the two paradigms. The network-native architectures activate
a larger fraction of compute nodes in every topology-model
pair, whereas LGD performs DNN computation only along
its selected deployment path. The difference becomes more
pronounced on the larger DAGs, where the network-native
architectures can exploit additional physical branches that are
unavailable to a single-path model-first deployment.
The network-native architectures also occupy a larger frac-
tion of the aggregate model-storage capacity across the evalu-
ated cases. This observation should not by itself be interpreted
as higher resource efficiency or better task performance.
Rather, it indicates that, under the same LGD-induced network
deadline, network-native architecture synthesis can convert
a broader portion of the distributed storage resources into
trainable model capacity, whereas LGD remains constrained
by its predefined architecture and selected deployment path.
Whether this additional architectural capacity translates into
improved task performance is examined in the subsequent
task-level comparison.

with complete reference DNNs deployed by LGD. For each
topology, LGD finds the minimum deployment latency of
each reference DNN which is the network-level inference

Figures 8 and 9 report peak top-1 test accuracies on
CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Each topology panel covers three
reference DNNs at three precision settings. LGD preserves
the reference DNNs during deployment. For a given dataset
and precision, each reference DNN has one baseline accuracy.
We use this value across all three topologies. The two fig-
ures contain 54 network-native models accuracy values and
18 distinct baseline values. For each dataset and precision
setting, Table V averages network-native models accuracy over
the nine topology and precision settings. The baseline mean
averages the three reference DNNs.
CIFAR-10. The network-native models achieve 88.40-93.50%
accuracy and exceed the baseline in 25 of 27 configurations.
The paired gains range from −0.99 to 6.31 percentage points,
with a mean gain of 2.31 percentage points across the 27 evalu-
ated configurations. The highest accuracy among the network-
native models is 93.50%, attained by the network-native model
synthesized under the ResNet50-matched deadline on Butter-
fly, compared with 90.70% for its FP32 baseline. All nine
network-native model configurations with ResNet18-matched
deadlines outperform their baselines, with accuracies of 91.89-
92.80%. Overall, the network-native models achieve accuracy
gains across all three reference DNNs in most configurations,
while remaining within one percentage point of the baseline
in the two exceptions.

71.81% accuracy and exceeds the baseline in all 27 config-

and have a descriptive mean of 5.71 percentage points, a
larger mean gap than on CIFAR-10. At FP32, the network-

native models synthesized under ResNet50-matched deadlines

The corresponding gains of 4.72, 5.67, and 5.97 percentage
points show that the advantage also occurs in the nominal FP32
setting. The FP32 gains are smaller for DenseNet121 (1.22-
1.95 percentage points) and ResNet18 (2.97-4.35 percentage
points), demonstrating that the improvement depends on the
reference-model family.
Precision and topology dependence. Table V shows positive
descriptive mean gains at all three nominal precisions. On
CIFAR-10, the reported mean gains are 1.53 percentage points
at FP32, 1.91 at 8-bit, and 3.49 at 4-bit. On CIFAR-100,
the corresponding gains are 3.47, 2.98, and 10.69 percentage
points. The largest reported mean gap occurs at nominal 4-bit
on CIFAR-100, where the baseline mean is 59.61% and the
network-native model mean is 70.30%. Relative to their FP32
means, these represent decreases of 7.63 and 0.41 percentage
points, respectively. For the network-native models on CIFAR-
10, the precision decreases 0.94 percentage points from FP32


--- Page 13 ---
13
to 4-bit. These differences are calculated from the rounded
table entries. Individual configurations do not always follow
the aggregate trend. These precision comparisons evaluate
fixed architectures rather than architectures independently syn-
thesized for each precision setting.
The topology ranking also changes with the reference
model and precision. For network-native models synthesized
under ResNet50-matched deadlines on CIFAR-10, Butterfly
has the highest FP32 accuracy, whereas Nobel-EU has the
highest 4-bit accuracy. On CIFAR-100 at FP32, Nobel-US
leads for ResNet18, while Butterfly leads for ResNet50 and
DenseNet121. Thus, the largest physical DAG does not con-
sistently yield the highest accuracy.
VIII. CONCLUSION
This paper developed a network-native DNN architecture
synthesis framework and an efficient algorithm for construct-
ing distributed neural architectures under physical-network
constraints. The results highlight an important insight: the
physical network can serve not only as the infrastructure
for executing neural computation, but also as a resource for
shaping the neural architecture itself. By exploiting distributed
computation and storage across the network, architecture
synthesis creates opportunities to utilize resources that may
remain underused when neural dependencies are fixed in
advance. The observed improvements in classification accu-
racy further suggest that this architectural flexibility can yield
benefits beyond resource utilization, extending to task-level
performance. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential
of treating neural architecture as a network-dependent design
variable, rather than a fixed input to deployment optimiza-
tion. This perspective opens a new avenue for distributed
intelligence, where neural architectures and the underlying
computing networks are designed as an integrated system.
